sectors.title: Container stowage and vessel capacity
decisions: Compare loading sequences and compatible slots across vessels and ports before proposing a stowage plan.
Keep containers with missing or inconsistent verified mass out of the ready-to-load plan.
Estimate rehandles and equipment time when berth arrival or discharge order changes.
capacity: Count 20- and 40-foot slot positions separately and record paired-slot conflicts. Total TEU does not establish physical fit.
Track metric tonnes per stack, hatch or deck zone; use vessel-specific structural and stability limits, not aggregate deadweight alone.
Count compatible powered reefer positions and simultaneous crane moves per hour. Include outages and shore power limits.
constraints: Where SOLAS verified gross mass requirements apply, use the signed verified mass in the stowage process; a booking weight is not a substitute. Verification is a condition of loading, not authority to load.
Use vessel-approved Cargo Securing Manual limits and applicable cargo separation rules. A general IMO reference does not supply clearance for a specific ship or commodity.
Keep port discharge order, permissible hatch passage, and terminal crane restrictions separate from fleet preferences such as minimizing rehandles.
failureModes: An open slot has insufficient stack mass margin or the wrong container length.
An available reefer box position has no usable power outlet.
A revised port sequence traps containers behind later-discharge cargo or invalidates planned weight distribution.
proofNeeded: Ship-approved bay plan with slot compatibility and blocked positions, mass ledger with verified gross mass and timestamps, and equipment windows.
Vessel-specific loading and stability calculation signed off through the vessel's approved procedures; a planner replay alone is not proof.

sources.label: IMO: Verification of gross mass of a packed container
IMO: Code of Safe Practice for Cargo Stowage and Securing

sectors.title: Grocery replenishment and warehouse slots
decisions: Place each lot in a usable slot and allocate replenishment windows without blocking aisles or picking faces.
Reserve temperature-controlled space and handling equipment as stock and trucks arrive in waves.
Compare a promotion against a normal day using peak-hour labor and dock demand, not just total distance.
capacity: Pallet positions by dimensions and load rating in kg; cubic metres and case facings do not establish weight capacity.
Available powered lift trucks and trained operator-minutes; clearance in metres at the equipment's required turning envelope.
Dock door-minutes, concurrent staging pallet positions and chilled or frozen positions by approved temperature band in °C.
constraints: Apply local workplace rules on cleared aisles and stable storage. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.176 is a US baseline where it applies, not a global aisle width or forklift load rating.
Keep site-required lot rotation, segregation, shelf rules, spill zones and promotional displays separate from regulation.
For US transport covered by FDA sanitary transportation requirements, match the food safety specification and agreed responsibilities; transport rules alone do not define warehouse shelf life.
failureModes: The bin is empty but the loaded pallet cannot be placed safely by available equipment.
Promotion volume fills staging before the dock window opens, blocking the receiving path.
A chilled lot physically fits in an ambient bay, but the approved handling conditions cannot be met.
proofNeeded: Rack and equipment rating records, bay dimensions, shift-qualified operators and scanned lot and expiry dates.
Distinct capacity and queue measurements for receiving, staging, storage and replenishment, with agreed temperature handling evidence.

sources.label: OSHA: 29 CFR 1910.176, handling materials
OSHA: Grocery warehousing storage guidance
FDA: Sanitary Transportation of Human and Animal Food final rule

sectors.title: Fleet duty cycles and depot charging
decisions: Assign routes to vehicles, then schedule charge slots against return times, departure deadlines and minimum reserve.
Compare charge sequencing versus added connectors or a service upgrade before attributing shortages to vehicle count.
Replan when a charger faults, a route runs late or consumption deviates from the duty-cycle estimate.
capacity: Vehicle energy in usable kWh and percent state of charge; connector output in kW and station occupancy in minutes.
Shared electrical service limits in kW or kVA as specified by the site engineer and utility, with building load in the same time intervals.
Route payload in kg and m³, driver and vehicle minutes, and depot parking positions. Include energy for auxiliary refrigeration or climate load.
constraints: Treat connector, vehicle acceptance limits, site electrical capacity and approved engineering settings as hard input boundaries; US DOE fleet guidance does not authorize electrical work.
Model employer reserve and priority policy separately from legal vehicle load, road access and driver rules. Confirm jurisdiction, journey and vehicle applicability before evaluating.
Do not assume that advertised charger power is sustained or that sessions can overlap on one connector; model derating and charge curves.
failureModes: Several vehicles start at once and exceed the site headroom even though each connector is within its rating.
Available energy covers mean route demand but misses reserve after cold weather or credible route delay.
The vehicle finishes charging, but the connector only appears compatible in the inventory and is not approved for that model.
proofNeeded: Route and energy telemetry, asset-to-connector compatibility matrix, session event logs, and approved utility/site headroom by interval.
Replay a charger outage and late depot return without letting an undercharged vehicle appear dispatchable.

sources.label: US DOE Alternative Fuels Data Center: Electric Vehicles for Fleets
US DOE Alternative Fuels Data Center: Electricity production and distribution

sectors.title: Airport gates, arrivals and ground services
decisions: Assign contact gates and remote stands by aircraft and handling readiness, preserving space for late arrivals.
Compare a nominal gate assignment with the resulting baggage, passenger and ground-team workload.
Evaluate multi-stand closures or an arrival wave while showing which demand needs manual handling.
capacity: Gate or stand occupancy in aircraft-minutes, apron frontage and clearances in metres, and equipment compatibility by aircraft family.
Passenger-processing capacity per 15 minutes by staffed checkpoint, corridor, bus, and eligible arrivals stream; a gate count is not passenger capacity.
Qualified ground-team and equipment minutes in the same location and time window, including transfer and reset time.
constraints: An empty stand still needs airport-approved aircraft and adjacent-stand compatibility plus applicable airport conditions. FAA terminal planning guidance supports design work; it is not airport certification or approval.
Use local airport and airline rules for international arrivals handling, baggage reclaim, stand closures and service equipment. Carry these as separately versioned site inputs.
Protect mandatory buffers and handling dependencies. Only then compare preferences such as contact-gate use, walk distances and towing effort.
failureModes: Large aircraft can fit each stand individually but cannot occupy neighboring stands at the same time.
Moving a flight to a remote stand frees a gate but saturates the coach queue or ground-team schedule.
Gate assignment is feasible while baggage or eligible passenger processing is over capacity during the same arrival burst.
proofNeeded: Airport-approved stand and adjacency matrix, terminal and baggage processing rates, ground equipment roster and staff qualifications.
Stale closure and adjacency data must hold a recommendation; replay the peak arrival bank and verify no shared resource is double booked.

sources.label: US FAA Advisory Circular 150/5360-13A: Airport Terminal Planning
US FAA: Airport Planning and Design

sectors.title: Commercial rental fleets and workshop capacity
decisions: Match contract-compatible vehicles to pickup windows, including return uncertainty and one-way transfers.
Schedule inspection, cleaning, maintenance and recall holds before any next handover.
Rebalance approved substitutes between branches without treating unavailable workshop resources as capacity.
capacity: Available vehicle-hours by branch, class and equipment; distinguish physically present assets from release-ready assets.
Workshop bay-hours by compatible lift rating and technician-hours by required skill, plus waiting parts and wash or preparation capacity.
Transfer driver and vehicle minutes, destination parking slots and booking slack after expected return.
constraints: Separate operator roadworthiness obligations from local contract promises and upgrade/substitute rules. DVSA guidance cited here is for commercial goods or passenger operators, not a universal rental law.
Use the applicable inspection and recall records; a calendar flag alone is not a roadworthy-release decision.
Allow an out-of-service asset to be moved for permitted servicing only if specifically authorized. Do not treat that movement as rental availability.
failureModes: An asset is assigned as soon as it returns but needs inspection, repairs or a recall remedy.
A substitution satisfies inventory count but fails class, capacity or contract compatibility.
A workshop has free bays but lacks a qualified technician or a required part, stranding several bookings.
proofNeeded: Asset state history, booking and substitution contract, parts plan, and technician/bay compatibility.
Signed first-use or equivalent evidence where it applies, recall and rectification trace, and a separate handover-release event.

sources.label: UK DVSA: Guide to maintaining roadworthiness for commercial goods and passenger vehicles
UK DVSA: Maintenance investigation guidance and evidence

sectors.title: Outpatient room and support-team coordination
decisions: Prepare rooms and support staff for appointments already approved by the service.
Reassign cleaning, reception coverage, and equipment preparation after a cancellation.
capacity: Ready room-minutes by room class and site, after setup and turnover.
Reception and support staff-minutes by shift; equipment units ready in each interval.
Booked slots, attended slots, and late cancellations as separate counts.
constraints: Service-owned appointment order and session limits remain fixed.
Preparation and turnover must fit resource windows; assigned equipment cannot overlap.
Respect the approved room setup without storing the reason for any adjustment.
failureModes: Treating appointment bookings as attended work conceals wasted slots.
A room exists on paper but cannot open because no support worker or equipment is available.
Rebooking consumes a later slot and can move backlog instead of eliminating it.
proofNeeded: Replay anonymized cancellations and turnover durations using aggregate arrival and attendance records.
Compare opening delays, unused ready room-minutes, held tasks, and gaps by location against the current operating schedule.

NHS England missed appointments guidance

sectors.title: School timetabling and specialist room allocation
decisions: Assign groups to class periods, qualified staff, and suitable rooms.
Rebuild a day after a closure without unnecessarily moving unaffected classes.
capacity: Seats per usable room by period; specialist lab or workshop stations are a separate limit.
Teacher periods and room-periods with setup/cleanup time deducted.
Whole-school net capacity is a planning reference, not a per-class room authorization.
constraints: No simultaneous double booking of the room, group, or supervising staff.
Use locally verified room designation, accessibility, safety capacity, and staff requirements.
Preserve locked periods and allow real travel time between buildings.
failureModes: Enough total seats but no qualifying lab permits the lesson.
Two rooms appear free while the only approved supervisor is elsewhere.
A single room outage forces avoidable changes across the entire day.
proofNeeded: Verify each assignment against the room inventory, timetable, and approved staff coverage.
Replay a room outage and compare unserved lessons, moved periods, and cross-building travel.

sources.label: Department for Education net capacity assessment guidance for England

sectors.title: Multi-location shifts and shared relief teams
decisions: Fill shifts across stores and departments using an approved relief pool.
Choose whether to fill a staffing gap with local cover, a transfer, or a human escalation.
capacity: Qualified person-hours per site, role, and time band.
Transfer travel-minutes, net duty time after breaks, and minimum concurrent role coverage.
Relief staff capacity counted once across all participating departments.
constraints: Only approved staff and site-specific competencies count towards coverage.
Keep break, leave, availability and site-opening rules distinct; use the validated local work-time profile.
Charge transfer time and preserve agreed schedules where feasible.
failureModes: Two departments use the same floating worker at the same time.
Coverage appears adequate at daily granularity but drops below minimum for a key interval.
A relief transfer removes coverage at the sending site.
proofNeeded: Compare roster-to-actual coverage, missed intervals, reassignment count and paid travel.
Independently validate site permissions, approved absence windows, and constraints before release.

Oracle workforce scheduling: departments and locations

sectors.title: Contact center capacity by queue, skill and interval
decisions: Allocate net staff capacity to voice, chat and deferred tickets.
Move coaching or back-office work when wait times rise, without overloading another queue.
capacity: Forecast offered contacts per 15 or 30 minutes and handling seconds including follow-up.
Net staffed agent-minutes after unavailable time, with channel-specific concurrency.
Deferred backlog count and age distribution tracked separately from live-queue service targets.
constraints: Only authorized skills, languages, and business units are substitutable.
Keep concurrent chat limits separate from single-call voice occupancy.
Observe coverage during breaks and preapproved protected time.
failureModes: Good daily coverage hides short queue peaks and missed targets.
One multilingual agent is counted at full capacity in two queues.
A voice-only objective pushes deferred work beyond its response target.
proofNeeded: Replay actual aggregate arrivals, staffing and handle times by channel and interval.
Compare queue wait distribution, target attainment, abandonment, oldest backlog and transfer load; no customer payloads needed.

sources.label: Genesys planning groups: queue, media, language and skill
Amazon Connect interval capacity planning

sectors.title: Transactional printing, insertion and handoff
decisions: Group compatible work around pickup cutoffs; reserve a rerun lane for damaged pieces.
Hold suspected duplicate or mismatched pieces before dispatch.
capacity: Press impressions per hour by stock and duplex mode; inserter pieces per hour by envelope and insert profile.
Setup and changeover minutes, reprint setup, check-station throughput and dispatch cutoff time.
Track usable stock by media lot and production stages, not only gross page count.
constraints: Check press/finisher compatibility and material availability before batching.
Keep a single verified release per piece identifier; preserve holds and reconciliation evidence.
Treat print-floor release and carrier acceptance as separate checks.
failureModes: Optimizing print runs alone moves the queue to insertion.
A fast rerun releases the original and replacement without deduplication.
A batch meets press schedule but misses carrier handoff.
proofNeeded: Replay historical job tickets and independent scan logs with duplicate, mismatch and missing events.
Reconcile verified pieces, holds and carrier documentation; compare waste, idle time and cutoff attainment.

sources.label: CIP4 job ticket and device capability references
USPS commercial mail verification and acceptance

sectors.title: Facilities maintenance and work-order backlog
decisions: Slot preventive and corrective work around staffed coverage and tenant access.
Replan the low-priority backlog when an urgent fault consumes a crew or a part is delayed.
capacity: Qualified technician-hours, shared lift/tool-hours, verified spare units and access-window minutes.
Separate travel and staging from hands-on work; keep callout capacity reserved.
constraints: Access and owner-approved safety prerequisites are gates, not scores.
Reserve a crew for multi-person jobs; count shared tools once.
Treat expected-part arrival and onsite confirmation differently; lock agreed facility windows as required.
failureModes: A visit is scheduled while the part, access permission, or owner signoff is missing.
Shared equipment ties up two otherwise workable crews.
Reactive work repeatedly displaces preventive work without recording the maintenance debt.
proofNeeded: Verify work-order readiness and closure with maintenance records, including reopened jobs.
Compare first-visit completion, overdue preventive items, return trips and unresolved urgent demand.

sources.label: U.S. Department of Energy facilities operations and maintenance challenges

sectors.title: DNS and load balancing
decisions: Choose the regions new DNS lookups can use.
Allocate incoming traffic to eligible services or keep excess demand unserved.
capacity: Requests or connections per second, active connections, and reserve capacity by region.
Independent failure domains with enough healthy capacity to absorb a shift.
constraints: Approved regions, probe freshness, required coverage after failure, and a reviewed fallback.
DNS cache lifetime, sticky sessions, and existing connections limit how quickly traffic moves.
failureModes: Stale health appears current; all targets fail and a provider returns an unhealthy destination; answer weights do not match request shares.
proofNeeded: Recorded probe and load snapshots with units and timestamps; test missing health, all-unhealthy pools, cache lag, and demand over capacity.
Compare DNS answer shares with actual request load as separate measurements.

sectors.title: Platform services and shared capacity
decisions: Set admit, queue, or defer limits per kind of work.
Keep headroom for critical work when a shared dependency slows down.
capacity: Downstream concurrent work, queue service rate, and spare capacity before the latency target is lost.
Retry volume and the amount of work one customer or service can consume.
constraints: Priority policy, maximum queue age, fairness across work streams, bounded retries and backoff.
Capacity that comes online after a delay cannot be counted as available now.
failureModes: Retries amplify overload; a queue appears healthy while work ages out; one tenant exhausts a shared worker pool.
proofNeeded: Measured queue and dependency telemetry, traffic recorded by priority, and an approved overload policy.
Replay a slow dependency, burst, and loss of a worker group; report deferrals and latency separately.

sectors.title: Cluster workload placement
decisions: Place workloads on nodes and zones that can run them.
Decide which work can wait during a drain, upgrade, or zone outage.
capacity: Schedulable CPU and memory, usable accelerators, compatible nodes, and placement room in each zone.
Headroom to reschedule work after a zone is unavailable.
constraints: Resource requests, supported hardware, required placement labels, incompatibilities and zone-spread policies.
Treat an unsatisfied hard spread rule as pending work, not a successful placement.
failureModes: The cluster has enough total capacity but no compatible node has enough free resources; an upgrade packs replicas into one zone.
proofNeeded: Versioned workload and node inventory with zone labels, resource units and policy scope.
Replay a drain and a missing zone; list pending workloads and the first failed constraint.

sectors.title: Multi-region recovery
decisions: Choose which region can take traffic and when a return is safe.
Prioritize services and data restoration when the standby cannot handle the full load.
capacity: Failover compute, storage write throughput, replication bandwidth, and dependencies that have warmed up.
Recovery time and tolerated data loss are separate targets.
constraints: Data placement policy, observed replication lag, allowed write leadership and service dependency order.
Require evidence that standby and critical dependencies are ready, not just a reachable endpoint.
failureModes: A standby can receive traffic but lacks key dependencies; separate sites accept conflicting writes; failback starts before the replica catches up.
proofNeeded: Recovery objectives approved per service, recent measured lag and restoration tests, and a versioned policy for switching writes.
Replay regional loss and delayed replication; report both time-to-restore and measurable recovery point.

AWS Well-Architected: Disaster recovery testing

sectors.title: Storage and network headroom
decisions: Choose where volumes can be placed alongside workloads.
Schedule data copies and backups without crowding out customer traffic.
capacity: Free capacity by storage class and zone, write throughput, input/output operations per second, and cross-zone link bandwidth.
Reserved bandwidth and time for periodic backups or replication.
constraints: Access mode, volume topology, data locality, per-link capacity, and approved backup windows.
Two paths are not independently resilient unless their shared infrastructure is understood.
failureModes: Free storage exists only in the wrong zone; a failed link overloads the remaining path; backup I/O displaces application writes.
proofNeeded: Topology-aware storage inventory, measured storage and link headroom, approved movement windows and a path dependency map.
Replay one unavailable zone and one degraded link without treating aggregate totals as usable capacity.

AWS Well-Architected: Dedicated connectivity considerations

sectors.title: Data-center power and cooling
decisions: Choose when and where to run power-intensive work.
Reserve capacity for mandatory load while deferring work that can wait.
capacity: Rack and circuit power in kilowatts, UPS and cooling reserve, and measured facility demand.
Available cooling and power after scheduled maintenance or equipment loss.
constraints: Engineer-approved electrical and cooling limits, vendor equipment limits, safe placement, and maintenance windows.
Keep carbon, cost, and energy goals separate from hard operating limits.
failureModes: One rack overheats while site-wide averages look safe; maintenance removes the redundancy counted in the plan; missing telemetry is mistaken for spare capacity.
proofNeeded: Meter-level readings, rack and circuit mapping, equipment ratings, and approved loss-of-equipment scenarios.
Test local constraints during equipment loss and report unmet load; no electrical safety approval from a worked case.

sectors.title: Water utility service restoration
decisions: Schedule restoration crews, temporary power and inspection windows after an incident.
Prioritize recovery against an approved utility response plan; do not operate controls.
capacity: Crew-hours by authorization, backup power kW, fuel runtime hours, inspection and sampling windows.
constraints: Use approved utility procedures and equipment ratings. Restoration and public notices stay with the responsible operator.
A standby generator rating is not a continuous duty rating.
failureModes: A repair is complete but inspection is not approved.
Extended outage exceeds standby generator or fuel assumptions.
Two work orders compete for the same temporary power unit.
proofNeeded: Approved service priorities, time-stamped crew/resource state, verified equipment ratings and a signed operator handoff.
Rehearse concurrent outages without publishing real facility topology.

EPA power resilience guide

sectors.title: Construction equipment and lift-window planning
decisions: Reserve crews and equipment around permit, delivery and weather windows.
Hold a proposed window when the required qualified review is missing.
capacity: Equipment hours, setup areas, spotters and supervisors, verified equipment-specific ratings.
constraints: Do not infer safe rated capacity from a nominal crane tonnage. A competent person addresses effects of wind, ice or snow under applicable OSHA rules.
Where OSHA's multiple-crane rule applies, use the approved plan and authorized lift director; scheduling software is not lift approval.
failureModes: Configuration changed after a plan was reviewed.
A delivery overruns and the site access window closes.
Two reservations need the same qualified director.
proofNeeded: Reviewed equipment configuration, current authorizations, reliable weather policy, permit windows, and explicit manual release.

OSHA multiple-crane lift rule

sectors.title: Cold-chain loading and receiving
decisions: Assign orders to compatible compartment windows, decide what to stage, and hold shipments lacking receiving or temperature evidence.
capacity: Compartment weight and volume, staged pallet spaces, dock door minutes, receiver capacity.
constraints: Use shipment-specific shipper conditions and pre-cooling evidence where required; no universal temperature threshold.
Distinguish shipper, loader, carrier and receiver responsibilities, including role agreements, exemptions and waivers where applicable.
failureModes: A sensor reading is stale or unavailable.
A booked receiver window closes while staging is still full.
A compartment fails and the remaining compartments cannot satisfy both weight and volume.
proofNeeded: Shipment and compartment evidence snapshots, documented responsibility, role-specific time boundaries, and a reviewer for excursions or missing evidence.
